judged_text: Credentials fetched from DB by raw ID with no ownership validation (`EventManager.ts:~341-357` and `~505-530`, `handleCancelBooking.ts:~425-441`): `prisma.credential.findUnique({ where: { id } })` uses whatever row comes back without checking that the credential belongs to the booking's user/hosts, expanding the trust boundary from fail-closed to fail-open — a malicious user could point their destination calendar at any credential ID in the database and have bookings write to or cancel/update another user's calendar using their OAuth tokens; needs explicit `userId`/`teamId` scoping on the DB fetch

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new fallback credential lookups by raw primary key with no user/team ownership scoping. In `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`, if a `destination.credentialId` isn’t found in `this.calendarCredentials`, it now calls `prisma.credential.findUnique({ where: { id: destination.credentialId } })` and then uses that credential to `createEvent(...)`. Similarly, in `EventManager.updateCalendarEvent` it does `findUnique({ where: { id: reference.credentialId } })` when the credential isn’t in `this.calendarCredentials`, and in `handleCancelBooking` it does `prisma.credential.findUnique({ where: { id: credentialId } })` if not found under `bookingToDelete.user.credentials`. These are exactly the patterns the finding describes: fetching “whatever row comes back” and then performing calendar operations with it, whereas previously missing credentials would effectively fail-closed (no DB fallback). The diff itself does not show any explicit `userId`/`teamId` check on these DB fetches.
